what_it_does: Many hardware side-channel attacks — methods that spy on a victim program by watching traces left in shared processor resources rather than reading its memory directly — fail in practice because the attacker cannot measure at a fine enough time scale to catch the moment a secret value is being processed. This paper introduces 'controlled preemption,' a technique available to an ordinary unprivileged (userspace) program that manipulates when the operating system interrupts a running process, effectively letting the attacker choose the precise moment their measurement code runs relative to the victim. By forcing preemption at attacker-chosen instants, the method dramatically sharpens the timing resolution of side-channel observations — making previously impractical attacks practical — without requiring any special privileges or hardware modifications. The paper treats this as a general amplification primitive: it does not exploit a specific bug but rather abuses normal OS scheduling mechanisms.
